title: Socrates and the Hemlock: The Trial of Athens
culture_region: India / Greece / USA / South Africa / World
summary: 'The unexamined life is not worth living', declared Socrates, refusing to trade his philosophical mission for cowardly exile, and drinking the fatal poison with serene courage.
keywords: Socrates and the Hemlock: The Trial of Athens
full_text:
In 399 BCE, the democratic court of Athens placed its greatest citizen on trial: seventy-year-old Socrates.

The indictment charged that he corrupted the Athenian youth by teaching them to question authority, and that he failed to worship the civic gods.

The judges offered a compromise: if he ceased his public philosophical inquiries in the marketplace, he would be spared.

Socrates stood before the five hundred jurors, his demeanor radiating tranquility:
"Men of Athens! I honor and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you.
As long as I have breath and strength, I will never cease from the practice of philosophy, urging every one of you:
Are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honor, while caring so little about wisdom, truth, and the greatest improvement of your soul?
**The unexamined life is not worth living!**"

Enraged by his uncompromising integrity, the court sentenced him to death by poison.

In his prison cell, his disciple Crito urged him to escape through a bribed guard. Socrates refused:
"To flee now because of fear of death would be to make a mockery of my seventy years of teaching obedience to the law. A philosopher does not run like a thief in the night."

When the jailer brought the cup of deadly hemlock, Socrates took it without trembling. Praying that his journey to the next world be blessed, he drank the poison as though it were water.

As his weeping disciples cried aloud, Socrates chided them gently:
"Be quiet and let me die in peace. They can destroy my physical body; but no poison can slay the immortal truth!"

With those words, Socrates transformed his martyrdom into the foundation stone of Western philosophy.
moral: Integrity means aligning our actions with truth, even when truth demands the ultimate sacrifice.
